candidates.title: Joint molecular optimization for efficient virtual screening via machine learning
candidates.abstract: Joint molecular optimization serves as the central focus of this research, which explores the synergistic integration of machine learning (ML) and virtual screening (VS) for drug discovery. This study addresses these limitations by integrating molecular docking and ML to predict and balance multiple molecular properties concurrently. Traditional VS methods often fall short by primarily targeting single molecular properties, such as binding affinity, overlooking the necessity of simultaneously optimizing multiple crucial parameters like ADMET (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity) profiles. Key objectives include developing and evaluating multi-objective optimization strategies and employing ML models (e.g., logistic regression, SVM, neural networks) to enhance predictive accuracy and computational efficiency. This research balances efficacy and safety metrics to refine VS and demonstrates the effect of combining these strategies on benchmark data. This work contributes a controlled, reproducible framework and an explicitly defined multi-objective prioritization procedure intended to support more efficient and transparent virtual screening, offering valuable insights for researchers in drug discovery, computational chemistry, and ML. Claims of reduced clinical attrition or improved clinical success would require prospective experimental validation and lie beyond the scope of this computational study.

candidates.title: Optimal-transport flow matching for stochastic model ipdating
candidates.abstract: Deep generative models have attracted considerable attention as inference engines for stochastic model updating. Among these deep generative models, conditional flow matching offers a particularly efficient formulation, in which a continuous transport map from a latent distribution to the posterior is learned by regression against optimal-transport probability paths, avoiding both the invertibility constraints of normalising flows and the iterative denoising of diffusion models. However, its performance in engineering model updating has not been examined against an established baseline such as the Bayesian updating framework under controlled conditions. In this work, conditional flow matching is therefore assessed against the Bayesian model updating approach with transitional Markov chain Monte Carlo, in which the Bhattacharyya distance provides the approximate likelihood for the Bayesian approach. The two methods are assessed with respect to posterior fidelity, evaluated by statistical distances against the known ground truth and computational expenditure in model evaluations, with the offline training budget reported separately from the inference cost of each subsequent conditioning. A 3-DOF spring–mass system with uncertain stiffness parameters serves as the benchmark. Since the calibrated posterior constitutes the input description upon which subsequent reliability assessment depends, the accuracy and the marginal cost of the updating step both bear directly on reliability computations. In addition, the amortised nature of the learned transport map is discussed in this work, as it permits the posterior to be re-evaluated under new observations at negligible cost, which is a property of practical relevance to reliability assessment under sequentially acquired monitoring data.

candidates.title: Beyond SELEX: AI-driven aptamers from sequence to structure to function.
candidates.abstract: Conventional aptamer discovery by systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX) is often constrained by limited library capacity, PCR bias, and multi-round screening. The recent convergence of artificial intelligence with aptamer development is driving a paradigm shift from empirical screening toward rational, data-driven design. This Review presents a timely and comprehensive overview of AI integration across the entire aptamer development pipeline, with a particular emphasis on advances reported in 2024-2026. We begin by discussing bioinformatics databases and computational tools for high-throughput SELEX data analysis. We then review state-of-the-art strategies for secondary and tertiary structure prediction, including recent breakthroughs such as AlphaFold 3, RoseTTAFoldNA, and diffusion-based approaches. We also cover machine learning methods for aptamer-target interaction prediction, molecular docking, dynamics simulations, and free energy calculations. A major focus is placed on very recent AI-driven generative design, including diffusion models (AptaDiff), language model-based frameworks (InstructNA, GRAPE-LM), and reinforcement learning approaches (AiDTA) for de novo aptamer generation and optimization. Emerging applications of AI-designed aptamers in precision diagnostics, targeted therapy, and biosensing are also surveyed. Finally, we discuss current challenges and outline future directions toward closed-loop, interpretable AI frameworks for translational aptamer development. By synthesizing the latest computational and experimental advances, this Review aims to serve as a timely resource for researchers seeking to leverage AI for next-generation aptamer discovery.

candidates.title: Targeted Protein Degradation: PROTACs, Molecular Glues, and the Future of Drug Discovery
candidates.abstract: The ability to selectively eliminate pathogenic proteins rather than merely inhibit their activity has redefined contemporary drug discovery, positioning targeted protein degradation (TPD) as one of the most significant advances in chemical biology and precision therapeutics.By harnessing endogenous protein quality-control machinery, TPD offers a catalytic and event-driven pharmacological strategy capable of addressing limitations associated with conventional occupancydriven inhibitors, including poor target selectivity, transient target engagement, acquired resistance, and the inaccessibility of many disease-relevant proteins.Among the expanding repertoire of degrader technologies, proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) and molecular glues have emerged as the most mature and clinically advanced platforms, each employing distinct mechanisms to recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases and direct selective protein degradation.Their rapid evolution has been driven by breakthroughs in structural biology, medicinal chemistry, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence, enabling the rational design of degraders with enhanced potency, selectivity, and pharmacokinetic performance.Beyond oncology, these technologies are increasingly being explored for neurological, inflammatory, infectious, and rare genetic disorders, underscoring their broad therapeutic potential.Nevertheless, challenges related to E3 ligase diversity, tissue specificity, resistance mechanisms, safety, and clinical translation continue to influence their successful implementation.This review critically examines the molecular foundations, design principles, therapeutic applications, and clinical progress of PROTACs and molecular glues while integrating emerging targeted degradation platforms and technological innovations.Furthermore, it discusses the opportunities and unresolved challenges that will shape the next generation of degrader therapeutics and their transformative role in the future of precision drug discovery.

candidates.title: OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling
candidates.abstract: Generative visual verifiers play a crucial role in advancing multimodal intelligence. To enhance the robustness of visual verifiers in complex multimodal scenarios involving compositional requirements, we move beyond conventional binary verifiers that produce only True/False discrete judgments and introduce a verifier that automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine-grained components and assigns pointwise scores to provide a continuous and more informative critique signal. Our experiments further demonstrate that these structured and interpretable outputs improve the verifier's generalization to out-of-domain multimodal critic tasks. To train this verifier, we introduce a Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise local feedback to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that provide a foundation for reliable continuous scoring at the global level. Under a general reinforcement learning framework, we first empirically demonstrate that the proposed pointwise graded verifier significantly outperforms binary verifiers in traditional text-to-image scenarios. We then extend our investigation to rule-governed generative world modeling where generative models are leveraged for world simulation and world reasoning under explicit rules. From a theoretical standpoint, we further show that a pairwise verification paradigm yields more accurate critiques than the pointwise formulation when ground-truth images are available, with empirical results on diverse structured world-modeling tasks such as Maze and Sudoku further validating the effectiveness of our approach. Overall, our findings suggest a key insight: the transition from generative models to structured world-modeling agents critically hinges on the availability of accurate pairwise graded visual verifiers.

candidates.title: Converting FGFR inhibitors into selective covalent molecular glue degraders via transposable gluing handles.
candidates.abstract: Molecular glue degraders (MGDs) have emerged as a transformative therapeutic modality, offering the potential to deplete undruggable or pathogenic proteins. However, the rational design of MGDs remains inherently challenging compared to traditional heterobifunctional degraders. Recently, the implementation of transposable chemical gluing handles has provided an efficient approach to convert established protein-targeting ligands into target-specific MGDs. In this study, by incorporating diverse molecular glue handles and amino acid-based degrons into the solvent-exposed exit vectors of infigratinib, we synthesized a library of 30 candidate MGDs. Preliminary screening and subsequent lead optimization identified LC-MG-5 and LC-MG-10 as highly efficient degraders of FGFR2. In cellular models, both compounds demonstrated potent suppression of FGFR2-mediated signaling pathways. Mechanistic investigations revealed that the covalent engagement of the gluing handle is a critical determinant for successful proteasomal degradation of FGFR2. This work provides a framework for the rational transformation of kinase inhibitors into covalent molecular glue degraders, underscoring the potential of FGFR degradation as a next-generation precision medicine strategy for FGFR2-driven malignancies.

candidates.title: Generative modeling of topological and spatiotemporal data
candidates.abstract: Structured data are central to modern machine learning systems, but their structure creates modeling challenges that are not present in flat vectors or single images: graphs are invariant to node ordering, visual scenes combine symbolic relations with continuous geometry, and human or driving motion evolves through interacting agents under uncertainty. This dissertation develops generative models for topological, hybrid, and spatiotemporal data by adapting how these models represent, learn, and sample structured distributions. The first part of this thesis studies topological and hybrid data. It begins with graph generation, where we bound the support of closest invariant distributions under explicit symmetry assumptions and characterize the symmetrized empirical target induced by equivariant denoising. Learning additional permuted representations can reduce performance in the studied settings. This motivates a graph diffusion model that combines flexible non-invariant denoising with permutation-invariant sampling and an efficient shifted-window graph transformer. We then extend this topological view to grounded scene graphs, where object categories, bounding boxes, and relations are generated jointly to bridge symbolic scene structure and continuous visual generation. The second part of this thesis studies motion forecasting. We formulate human trajectory prediction as conditional flow matching, enabling correlated multimodal futures to be generated together as scene-level hypotheses. We then scale this approach to autonomous-driving motion prediction by jointly producing multiple trajectories, learning confidence rankings, and improving generalization via self-conditioning. Together, these works show that generative models for structured domains become useful when structure is handled explicitly but flexibly, and identify opportunities for unified structured world models, faster samplers, and uncertainty-aware deployment.

candidates.title: Poisoning the corpora of protein design systems during pre-training and retrieval
candidates.abstract: Protein foundation models increasingly support the generation of novel biological sequences, yet their reliance on large public datasets creates opportunities for adversarial manipulation of the material they learn from and retrieve. We investigate two data-only poisoning attacks against protein design systems, targeting the pre-training corpus of autoregressive protein language models and the retrieval corpus of a text-guided protein generator. For the first, we pre-trained ProtGPT2 and ProGen2 variants of 300 million parameters, introducing poisoned protein sequences containing one of two triggers followed by one of three payloads. Across all poisoned runs, both architectures acquired highly reliable trigger-dependent generation under uniform and ramped poisoning schedules. Under ramped exposure, the earliest majority activation occurred after only 200 contaminated examples, while for the uniform schedule earliest activation occurred around 5000 poisoned samples. For the second attack, we inserted records into a retrieval corpus system without modifying its weights or decoding procedure. A single query-aware record captured a top-16 retrieval position for 58\% of templated requests and 97\% of free-text requests. Conditional on successful poisoned retrieval, 62\% of requests produced altered sequences, while 19-21% acquired the inserted domain by profile-HMM homology. A universal query-unaware attack using 1,500 records also achieved substantial retrieval capture and domain transfer. Together, these findings demonstrate that adversarial protein sequence contributions can establish persistent, sequence-specific behaviour during pre-training or redirect protein generation at inference, while leaving ordinary model behaviour largely preserved. Our work establishes the integrity and biological provenance of protein sequence data as critical safeguards for generative protein design systems.

candidates.title: Conditional diffusion-based inverse kinematics for redundant 7-DOF manipulators with differentiable refinement
candidates.abstract: Background Inverse kinematics of redundant manipulators is a multi-solution problem, since one end-effector pose may correspond to multiple admissible joint configurations. Classical numerical solvers and regression-based neural models usually return a single joint configuration and therefore do not explicitly represent the inverse-kinematic solution manifold. Existing generative solvers based on normalizing flows produce multiple solutions, but they require invertible network architectures and do not include an explicit task-space correction stage. This study aimed to develop a hybrid generative-kinematic method for inverse kinematics of a redundant 7-DOF manipulator that can generate multiple admissible configurations for a given target pose. Methods A hybrid method, DiffusionIK, was developed by combining conditional diffusion-based generation, classifier-free guidance, DDIM sampling, and differentiable forward-kinematics refinement. A ResMLP denoiser is trained in the normalized joint space using procedurally generated training pairs obtained from the forward kinematics of the xArm manipulator. For each target pose, the diffusion model generated multiple candidate joint configurations, and the refinement stage subsequently reduced the task-space residual for each candidate. Numerical experiments were performed on 500 reachable target poses with 50 generated candidates per pose. Performance was evaluated using position and orientation success thresholds of 1 mm and 1°, respectively, together with the preservation of joint-space variability after refinement. Results DiffusionIK reached 99.40% success after 200 refinement steps and 100.00% after 500 steps under 1 mm and 1° thresholds, with a mean joint-space variability of 9.77 rad. In a unified benchmark against damped least squares, KDL, direct regression, and a normalizing-flow baseline, DiffusionIK with refinement achieved 99.80% success on 500 unseen poses and 98.40% near singularities, matching the strongest numerical solver while returning 50 diverse solutions per pose. Conclusion The proposed DiffusionIK method provides an effective formulation of redundant inverse kinematics as conditional generation followed by local kinematic correction. By combining diffusion-based candidate generation with differentiable forward-kinematics refinement, the method represents the multi-solution nature of redundant manipulators and achieves high task-space accuracy while preserving configuration diversity. Unlike normalizing-flow-based solvers, DiffusionIK imposes no invertibility constraints on the denoiser and combines generation with differentiable forward-kinematics refinement, which provides sub-millimetre and sub-degree accuracy together with configuration diversity.

candidates.title: Query-Efficient Rejection Sampling for Parallel Masked Diffusion
candidates.abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) accelerate generation by unmasking multiple tokens in parallel, but sampling these tokens independently ignores their correlations and biases the output. Anari et al. (2026) corrected this bias with rejection sampling, decomposing the log acceptance probability into a sum of token-level terms, but the evaluation requires one score query per unmasked token. We propose the Single-Increment Rejection Sampler (SIRS), which provides an estimate of the log acceptance probability from a single randomly sampled increment at the cost of one query. SIRS then converts a Poisson number of clipped estimates into accept/reject decisions through a Bernoulli factory adapted from Chen et al. (2026). Since each query returns the conditionals of all remaining tokens in the block, we further Rao-Blackwellize each increment by averaging over these tokens at no extra cost, thereby reducing clipping. We show that the KL-divergence between the data distribution and the SIRS output is bounded by a clipping term plus the model's training error. With exact scores, parallel decoding pays the full within-block dependence, whereas SIRS pays only the part beyond the clipping range.

candidates.title: PathFM: Fast Generative Forecasting of Multivariate Trajectories
candidates.abstract: Time series foundation models are becoming increasingly popular for general-purpose forecasting. However, most leading models predict marginal quantiles, leaving the dependence structure of future trajectories unspecified. This distinction matters for trajectory-dependent quantities such as cumulative demand, peak load, and event timing, yet point and marginal scores do not reveal it. To model this dependence, we introduce PathFM, a trajectory-based forecasting model that uses flow matching to generate complete future paths. We further distill the model to one or two steps and share history attention cache across draws. Together, these enable PathFM to generate multiple paths for a single series in roughly the time needed for one query to a quantile model. The distilled sampler also makes it practical to optimize a calibration loss directly. PathFM achieves competitive marginal accuracy on the established forecasting benchmarks fev-bench and TIME. To complement these evaluations, we introduce Forecast Path Score Bench (fps-bench), which augments fev-bench tasks with energy and variogram scores and downstream metrics. PathFM achieves a higher aggregate path score on fps-bench than all evaluated external baselines. Experiments on chaotic systems further show that our flow model sustains long-run variability, while strong baselines rapidly collapse. PathFM makes generative time series forecasting both competitive and practical, enabling diverse downstream applications.

candidates.title: LLM‐Assisted Design of Ultralow‐κ Chalcogenides
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT Accelerating the discovery of materials with extreme lattice thermal conductivity () is limited by the high cost of first‐principles screening. Here, we develop an LLM‐assisted low‐ discovery workflow, where Bayesian optimization (BO) proposes candidates, an LLM performs evidence‐conditioned re‐ranking, and physics‐based structure generation, stability validation, and calculations serve as the acceptance criteria. This integration enables efficient candidate prioritization while maintaining rigorous physical validation. The workflow identifies dynamically stable Ag‐based chalcogenides, including Ag 3 SbSe 4 , Ag 4 TiSe 4 , and Ag 4 TiTe 4 . Mechanistic analysis reveals that their ultralow originates from strong phonon renormalization and coherence‐dominated heat transport. Ag 3 SbSe 4 is predicted to reach a maximum of 2.94 at 500 K due to its ultralow of 0.11 W . Furthermore, automated high‐throughput screening of ternary compounds containing 14 elements identifies 2742 dynamically stable materials with W . These results demonstrate that evidence‐conditioned LLM re‐ranking effectively enhances BO‐driven, physics‐validated materials discovery.

candidates.title: A potent macrocyclic peptide binder enables effector-free crystallization of the GTPase RAB27A
candidates.abstract: RAB27A is a member of a highly conserved family of small GTPases that regulate intracellular vesicle trafficking. Multiple studies have linked RAB27A cellular activity to exosome-mediated modulation of the tumour microenvironment and inflammatory signalling, highlighting it as an attractive target for drug discovery. However, identifying structurally validated and selective inhibitors of the RAB27A-effector interaction has proven challenging, partly because wild-type RAB27A crystallizes only in complex with effector proteins such as Slp2a. Using mRNA display, we identified macrocyclic peptide ligands that target the RAB27A effector-binding interface. Optimisation of initial hits led to IMP2660, a nanomolar-affinity RAB27A binder that effectively disrupts RAB27A-effector interactions. IMP2660 enabled determination of a 2.1[A] structure of active-state RAB27A bound to a noncovalent macrocyclic peptide in the absence of an effector, revealing structural features of the effector-binding surface and providing a platform for future structure-guided ligand development.

candidates.title: Performance Analysis of Ensemble and Hybrid Deep Learning Models in Predicting Agricultural Chemical Residues and Crop Outcome
candidates.abstract: The contemporary agricultural system has substantially transformed its productivity through extensive deployment of chemical pesticides, herbicides, and fertilizers. However, these practices introduce significant environmental sustainability concerns and human health risks. This paper conducts a comprehensive performance analysis of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques, with emphasis on ensemble and hybrid architectures, applied between 2018 and 2025 to investigate the relationship between agricultural chemical usage, crop yield outcomes, and human health consequences. Through systematic review of 26 peer-reviewed publications selected via PRISMA guidelines, this study evaluates convolutional neural networks (CNNs), long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, hybrid CNN-LSTM architectures, random forests, gradient boosting machines, and probabilistic models. Experimental findings demonstrate that CNN-LSTM hybrid models achieve R² > 0.93 for crop yield prediction, while Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) attain AUC scores up to 0.91 for health risk assessment. Multi-objective optimization frameworks combining NSGA-II with reinforcement learning yield Pareto-optimal chemical application strategies. Key challenges

candidates.title: Rethinking Successive Rejects Algorithms
candidates.abstract: In the best-arm identification problem, an algorithm adaptively selects arms to find the arm of the largest mean reward. Successive Rejects (SR) is a simple fixed-budget best-arm identification algorithm that eliminates one candidate arm at each phase. At first glance, SR seems to have limited adaptivity, since it follows predetermined phase lengths. However, for Gaussian arms with common variance, SR's worst-instance error exponent normalized by the popular complexity measure $H_1(P)$ is optimal up to a constant factor, which partly explains why SR's performance is competitive compared with state-of-the-art adaptive sampling algorithms. In this paper, we extend the framework of SR by optimizing its predefined schedule of phase lengths. We formulate phase-schedule design as an optimization problem for the normalized error exponent. Then, we introduce a version of SR with the optimized schedule, which we call $H_1$-balanced Successive Rejects ($H_1$-SR). This schedule is optimal within the class of SR-type algorithms with deterministic equal-count schedules. For Gaussian arms with common variance, $H_1$-SR achieves at least $11/12$ of the optimal normalized rate over all adaptive algorithms for every $K\ge2$, and this approximation ratio converges to one as $1-O(1/\log K)$ as $K\to\infty$. This is a significant improvement over original SR, whose corresponding fraction of the optimal normalized rate converges to $1/4$. Finally, experiments on ten synthetic instances and two dataset-derived Gaussian benchmarks compare the optimized schedule with original SR at finite horizons. They show substantial gains on many instances while also exposing a regime in which more aggressive early elimination is costly.

candidates.title: Inverse materials design via joint generation of crystal structures and local electronic descriptors
candidates.abstract: Inverse design of inorganic crystals, in which structures are generated to satisfy a target property while preserving diversity and physical plausibility, remains more demanding than ab initio generation, as property conditioning can degrade the structural quality that current generative models otherwise achieve. We propose a diffusion framework that jointly denoises crystal-structure variables and site-resolved local electronic descriptors through a shared score network. As representative descriptors, we adopt Bader charge and atomic density of states (atomic DOS). Under band-gap- and formation-energy-conditioned generation, as well as their simultaneous combination, the joint models achieve higher success rates than the structure-only baseline in most target conditions, while also increasing the fraction of generated structures that satisfy uniqueness, novelty, thermodynamic stability, and physical validity. Control experiments with noise-corrupted Bader charges and with a physically uninformative dummy variable show that these gains require the jointly generated variable to faithfully reflect the true local electronic structure. The generated Bader charges agree with DFT references with an MAE of 5.4 × 10 −2 e on stable, unique and novel structures, and the generated atomic DOS captures the coarse spectral profile of the DFT reference around the median of its accuracy distribution, although finer details and accuracy vary with elemental species. These results establish local electronic descriptors as effective generative variables that serve two complementary roles: broadening the explored materials space through increased structural diversity, and mitigating the trade-off between property targeting and structural quality by guiding the structural trajectory toward electronically plausible configurations during joint denoising.

candidates.title: Bayesian Inverse Optimisation under Uncertainty Posterior Inference for Hidden Decision Objectives
candidates.abstract: Inverse optimization seeks the hidden objective that explains observed decisions, yet existing methods typically recover a single objective and ignore uncertainty in the underlying preferences. We develop a Bayesian framework that represents the unknown objective by a posterior distribution, combining a boundedrationality choice model with prior information to quantify uncertainty directly. We establish geometric conditions for identifiability, prove posterior consistency, derive the optimal n−1/2, contraction rate, obtain a Bernstein–von Mises approximation, and present a finite-sample concentration bound together with a robust fractional posterior for misspecified behavioural models. Posterior inference is performed using gradient-based Markov chain Monte Carlo and a Laplace approximation. Simulation studies demonstrate accurate recovery under noisy, misspecified, nonlinear, and high-dimensional settings, while a controlled clinical example illustrates uncertainty quantification in hidden decision preferences. The proposed framework extends inverse optimization from point estimation to statistically principled uncertainty quantification, providing a rigorous foundation for learning decision objectives from imperfect observations.

candidates.title: Molecular Docking an In Vitro Anticonvulsant evaluation of Newly Synthesized Substituted Phthalimide Schiff bases derivatives targeting GABAA receptor
candidates.abstract: Epilepsy, a chronic neurological disorder affecting nearly 50(million people worldwide, remains difficult to manage due to drug resistance and adverse effects of existing antiepileptic drugs. This study investigates phthalimide-based Schiff base derivatives as potential anticonvulsant agents targeting the gamma-aminobutyric acid type(A (GABAA) receptor. Fifteen derivatives were designed and screened using computer-aided drug design (CADD) and molecular docking simulations against the GABAA receptor (PDB(ID:(6X3X). The top five compounds (A1–A5) were shortlisted based on docking affinity, interaction with key residues, drug-likeness, ADME properties and predicted toxicity. In-silico analyses using Swiss ADME, BOILED-Egg, and Pro Tox-II indicated favorable pharmacokinetic profiles, blood–brain barrier permeability, and low toxicity. Visualization through BIOVIA(Discovery(Studio revealed stable hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interactions with residues TYR160, PHE77 and SER205. In-vitro assays using HepG2 cells confirmed dose-dependent activity comparable to phenytoin. The integrated computational and experimental approach demonstrated that these derivatives possess strong binding affinity, good oral bioavailability and minimal toxicity. Overall, the findings highlight phthalimide Schiff base derivatives as promising multifunctional candidates for anticonvulsant therapy, offering improved safety and efficacy profiles for future pharmaceutical development.

candidates.title: Lean Graph Search for Formal Theorem Proving
candidates.abstract: Retrieving relevant lemmas is crucial for formal theorem proving, enabling provers to build machine-checkable proofs from established mathematical results. Recent retrieval systems match library declarations to a target theorem or its intermediate proof steps, but make limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations. These dependencies can reveal supporting lemmas that are not necessarily lexically similar to the target theorem but recur in proofs of related problems. To this end, we propose LeanGraphSearch, a graph-based retrieval method for Lean 4 that constructs a graph from Mathlib's forward dependencies and traverses it to uncover supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependency chains. Specifically, LeanGraphSearch links each declaration to the premises it depends on, uses a graph-based ranking algorithm to propagate relevance from semantically matched declarations to their dependencies, and reranks the expanded candidates against the original query. Across two mathematical retrieval benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves recall by up to 12% over the strongest baseline, LeanSearch v2, on MathlibQR and increases coverage of complete annotated proof routes on MathlibMPR, covering up to 3.7% of extra groups. More importantly, we evaluate whether these retrieval gains translate into improved end-to-end theorem proving by integrating LeanGraphSearch into an iterative proving loop guided by Lean feedback. Across three theorem proving benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves pass rate at {8, 16, 32} reflection turns by as much as 40% compared to vanilla prover and at most 10% compared to LeanSearch v2, showing higher accuracy-cost efficiency. These findings highlight the value of dependency graph search for theorem proving and motivate further research on structure-aware search for proof discovery.

candidates.title: Deterministic, branch-selective optimization of peptidomimetic scaffolds reveals design principles for targeting TNF-α.
candidates.abstract: Tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) is a central driver of chronic inflammatory diseases, yet the development of non-biologic TNF-α inhibitors remains challenging due to the large, shallow nature of its protein-protein interface. Peptides offer a promising alternative to small molecules; however, rational optimization of complex peptide architectures such as branched or cyclic scaffolds remains a major bottleneck, as conventional approaches often rely on empirical screening or low-resolution mutagenesis. Here, we report a deterministic, branch-selective optimization strategy for a lysine-centered branched peptidomimetic TNF-α inhibitor using On-Demand Array Synthesis and Screening (ODAST). Through three iterative rounds of hypothesis-driven diversification, we systematically resolved the roles of charge identity, charge density, and cooperative aromatic interactions across distinct branches of the scaffold. This process led to the identification of a conserved bidentate anionic recognition motif, paired with aromatic and hydrogen-bonding elements that cooperatively stabilize TNF-α binding. The optimized peptides exhibited >10-fold improvements in apparent affinity and effectively inhibited TNF-α-induced cytotoxicity, with a lead compound displaying low-micromolar cellular IC

candidates.title: Grounding Generative Verification in 3D Content
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and 3D generation have expanded 3D understanding and synthesis. However, beyond visual fidelity, task-specific correctness grounded in 3D evidence remains a major challenge. We argue that building reliable 3D systems requires not only stronger generation and reasoning, but also verification feedback that identifies unmet requirements and explains their violations, allowing systems to reflect on and refine their outputs. Such feedback must integrate multi-view observations and distinguish genuine inconsistencies from projection-dependent appearances. We make three contributions. First, we introduce 3DVerifierBench, a benchmark spanning 10 tasks that evaluates decisions, rejection explanations, and responses to controlled changes in specifications and candidates. A human study reveals a 21.6 percentage-point gap between humans and the strongest tested model, GPT-6 Astra, while explanation-aware analysis exposes weaknesses in rejection reliability. Second, we analyze verification across fine-grained factual categories, exposing errors in values and target binding. We develop a scalable pipeline combining multi-view fact extraction, controlled 3D editing, and native annotations to produce 14,126 training examples with contradiction explanations and linked counterfactuals. Third, we examine how verification could support 3D generation through candidate selection and recursive refinement. In human-labeled sixteen-candidate pools, oracle selection improves complete factual success from 26.7% to 90.0%. In a separate eight-input study, human-guided recursive refinement satisfies all seven requirements for every input, compared with three under parallel Oracle@8. Together, our benchmark, analysis, and data pipeline establish a foundation for models to reflect on 3D content through reliable verification feedback.

candidates.title: Sequence-based artificial intelligence-guided inhibitory peptides to counteract AAV neutralizing antibodies in gene therapy.
candidates.abstract: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors have demonstrated strong clinical efficacy across multiple monogenic disorders, yet neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) remain major barriers to vector redosing and durable transduction. To address this limitation, we developed a sequence-based artificial intelligence framework integrating Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) and Evolutionary Scale Modeling with Low-Rank Adaptation (ESM-LoRA) to identify human-tolerant, virus-specific motifs across human and viral proteins using sliding-window analyses and multi-layer fine-tuning. Using capsid-derived segments from AAV2 and AAV843, we prioritized surface-accessible, virus-polarized peptides as candidate decoys and evaluated their ability to block AAV-targeted antibodies. The models achieved high accuracy in distinguishing human versus viral fragments, and selected peptides bound AAV-specific antibodies with nanomolar affinity, competitively restored capsid binding, and recovered >60% of baseline transduction in the presence of NAbs. In mouse models with pre-existing or redosing-induced antibodies, coadministration of decoy peptides and an IgG-degrading enzyme reduced high-titer NAbs to approximately 1:4 and restored hepatic transgene expression without detectable inflammatory or peptide-specific immune responses. A contrastive variational autoencoder (VAE) further generated non-natural peptides with broader epitope coverage. These results support sequence-driven AI design of short, low-immunogenicity decoy peptides as a translational strategy to mitigate NAb interference and enhance the feasibility of AAV redosing.

candidates.title: MAOMAO: an ontology-guided FAIR resource for harmonized peptide toxicity data
candidates.abstract: Therapeutic peptides have emerged as a rapidly expanding class of biomolecules with applications spanning antimicrobial, antiviral, anticancer, immunomodulatory, metabolic, and diagnostic settings (8). Their high target specificity, favorable safety profiles, and growing clinical success have positioned them as attractive alternatives or complements to traditional small-molecule therapeutics (36). The number of experimentally characterized bioactive peptides has therefore increased substantially during the last decade (38), supporting the development of specialized databases and computational resources for peptide discovery, functional annotation, and rational design (5,15,31,35). Despite these advances, toxicity remains a major limitation to peptide development and clinical translation, constraining candidate selection during early-stage screening and optimization (3).Peptide toxicity encompasses a broad spectrum of adverse biological effects that arise from the interaction between peptides and biological systems. Most toxicity phenotypes are routinely evaluated during peptide development including cytotoxicity, hemolysis, neurotoxicity, embryotoxicity, and ichthyotoxicity (19,27). These toxicity endpoints have direct implications for efficacy, safety, dosage, and regulatory approval. Toxicity annotations have consequently accumulated across public databases (31,18,24), literature-derived resources (26,29,28,34), supplementary datasets (9,4,23), and experimental studies (33,39). However, these resources remain fragmented, employ heterogeneous terminology and annotation criteria, and provide variable levels of metadata and evidence quality (21). Their development for distinct biological objectives further complicates integration, reproducibility, and large-scale analysis (17).The growing availability of toxicity data creates opportunities for computational toxicology, data-driven peptide engineering, and large-scale biological analyses (32). Their utility, however, depends on the quality, consistency, and transparency of the underlying data (14,7). Annotation ambiguity, conflicting evidence, heterogeneous endpoint definitions, incomplete metadata, and limited provenance tracking can reduce reproducibility and complicate downstream reuse (1). The FAIR principles-Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability-provide a framework for organizing and distributing scientific data to support discovery, integration, reproducibility, and long-term reuse (22). Nevertheless, a standardized framework that harmonizes heterogeneous peptidetoxicity annotations while preserving evidence, provenance, and metadata remains largely unavailable (21). FAIR-oriented resources tailored to both biological interpretation and computational reuse are therefore still needed (37,13).To address these limitations, we developed MAOMAO (Metadata-Aware Ontology for Multi-source Annotation Organization), an ontology-guided resource integrating peptide-toxicity information from public databases, literature-derived resources, and curated datasets. MAOMAO standardizes toxicity terminology, preserves source-level provenance, distinguishes uncertainty-related evidence states, and organizes annotations within a unified hierarchical framework. The resource also provides harmonized metadata, descriptor-based representations, protein language model embeddings, benchmark resources, and supporting documentation. These components establish a FAIR-oriented and reusable foundation for biological interpretation, computational toxicology, and predictive modeling of peptide toxicity.The workflow used to construct MAOMAO is summarized in Figure 1A. Toxicity-related information from heterogeneous sources was preprocessed, harmonized, mapped to a unified toxicity ontology, evaluated for annotation conflicts and evidence quality, enriched with standardized metadata, and consolidated into the final resource. To support dissemination, computational reuse, and long-term maintenance, MAOMAO was organized into a modular architecture comprising complementary resource layers (Figure 1B).MAOMAO was constructed by integrating toxicity-related information from publicly available databases, literature-derived resources, supplementary datasets, and manually curated repositories. Candidate resources were identified through a structured exploration of the peptide toxicity landscape using scientific search engines, bibliographic repositories, specialized peptide databases, review articles, and citation tracking (2,16). Searches combined general terms, including peptide toxicity, toxic peptides, toxic peptide databases, and toxic peptide predictive models, with endpoint-specific queries for hemolytic peptides, cytotoxic peptides, cytolytic peptides, neurotoxic peptides, embryotoxic peptides, ichthyotoxic peptides, and anti mammalian cells peptides. Additional resources were identified from toxicity prediction tools, benchmark datasets, supplementary materials, associated repositories, and specialized peptide resources. Searches were conducted using Google Scholar and PubMed (6) between June 2025 and September 2026 and covered resources available through September 2026.Candidate resources were evaluated according to predefined eligibility criteria, including relevance to at least one MAOMAO toxicity endpoint, availability of peptide sequences with corresponding categorical toxicity annotations or quantitative toxicity measurements, sufficient provenance information, and the possibility of programmatic or manual retrieval. Resources were excluded when the underlying dataset could not be retrieved through the reported publication, supplementary material, repository, or web server, or when the available material lacked sequences suitable for sequence-level integration. This included resources containing only numerical representations, peptide names, or functional annotations without the corresponding sequences. Candidate-source screening, eligibility decisions, integrated and excluded resources, and source-specific exclusion reasons are detailed in Supplementary Section S1. (A) Ontology-guided harmonization workflow used to construct the resource. Toxicity-related information collected from public databases, literature-derived datasets, and curated resources undergoes preprocessing, terminology harmonization, ontology mapping, evidence integration, quantitative-property parsing, and metadata harmonization to generate a standardized and provenance-aware toxicity resource. (B) Modular architecture of MAOMAO. The resource is organized into complementary layers comprising harmonized toxicity annotations, numerical toxicity properties, sequence profiles, and metadata (Core Layer), sequence-derived descriptors (Descriptor Layer), protein language model embeddings (Embedding Layer), benchmark resources (Benchmark Layer), practical usage examples, and supporting documentation (Documentation Layer). Together, these components establish a FAIR-oriented and reusable resource for peptide toxicity research.Data acquisition combined direct database downloads, repository and supplementary-file retrieval, and manual extraction when required. Retrieved records were converted into a standardized intermediate representation, preserving peptide sequences, toxicity annotations, quantitative toxicity measurements when available, source identifiers, literature references, and available metadata. Source-level quality control verified the reported access route, the availability of primary sequences and interpretable toxicity information, and the associated publication or repository. Records lacking peptide sequences, containing toxicity information that could not be interpreted, or presenting irrecoverable formatting inconsistencies were excluded. Retained records were then forwarded to preprocessing, terminology harmonization, ontology mapping, metadata harmonization, and evidence integration.Following data collection, records underwent standardized preprocessing to support integration across heterogeneous resources (Figure 1A). This stage included sequence validation, format standardization, annotation parsing, identifier normalization, and quality control. The final resource was restricted to peptides containing the 20 canonical amino acids and lengths between 5 and 70 residues (38,25). Recoverable formatting inconsistencies were corrected, exact duplicates within each source were removed, and identical sequences reported by different sources were retained to preserve provenance and support evidence integration. Each normalized sequence was assigned a deterministic identifier generated by applying SHA-256 to the UTF-8 encoding of the uppercase, whitespace-free sequence. Quantitative HC50, LC50, LD50, and MHC observations were parsed while preserving their reported relation, value, unit, and provenance, and were linked to Core sequences through this identifier. Detailed sequence-processing, identifier-construction, and quantitative-property procedures are provided in Supplementary Section S1.To prevent terminology inconsistencies during cross-source integration, toxicity-related annotations were examined for alternative spellings, synonyms, endpoint-specific descriptions, and sourcedependent nomenclature referring to equivalent biological concepts. These variants were mapped to a standardized vocabulary while preserving their original biological meaning. For example, haemolytic was normalized to hemolytic, and cytolytic to cytolysis.Harmonized annotations were mapped to the MAOMAO toxicity ontology, centered on the root category Toxic. The ontology comprises Cytotoxic, Neurotoxic, Embryotoxic, and Ichthyotoxic as primary classes, with Hemolytic, Cytolysis, and Anti mammalian cells represented as subclasses of Cytotoxic. Hemolytic denotes toxicity involving erythrocyte lysis, whereas Cytolysis captures cell lysis or membrane-disruptive activity without a specified cell type. Anti-mammalian-cell activity denotes damage to mammalian cells or reduced cell viability (20,30,40). The vocabulary was restricted to distinct toxicity concepts supported by retrievable sequence-level evidence. Complete endpoint definitions, mappings, and assignment rules are provided in Supplementary Section S2.Following data collection, harmonization, and ontology mapping, annotations associated with identical peptide sequences were aggregated across sources (Figure 1A). Because the same sequence could be reported with different toxicity annotations, an evidence-management framework was applied to classify each peptide-endpoint pair as positive, negative, ambiguous, unlabeled, or no information. Positive states represented direct or hierarchy-supported toxicity evidence, whereas negative states corresponded to direct endpoint-specific non-toxic evidence. Ambiguous states captured conflicting or unresolved annotations. Unlabeled states denoted sequences retained in endpoint-specific sources without an explicit class assignment, while no information indicated the absence of evidence for that endpoint.Negative evidence was further classified as strong or weak according to the supporting information available in the original source. Strong negatives were explicitly supported by experimental evidence, whereas weak negatives originated from randomly selected negative sets or lacked confirmation of the absence of toxicity annotations. Evidence strength was retained in the metadata and provenance records, enabling downstream analyses to account for confidence, uncertainty, and conflicting evidence. Definitions, assignment criteria, and conflict-resolution rules are provided in Supplementary Section S2.To support transparency, interoperability, and long-term reuse, source-and endpoint-level metadata were normalized into a unified schema. Harmonized fields included source identifiers, literature references, organism information, annotation provenance, retrieval dates, file formats, and version information when available. Missing values were explicitly preserved without inference. The schema also retained original source labels, ontology mappings, evidence categories, publication references, and resource-specific annotations, providing a standardized representation of the integrated biological and technical information.Provenance was maintained by linking harmonized annotations to their source-specific processed datasets, endpoint-integration outputs, and metadata records. The sequence-level pivot provides the harmonized access layer, while provenance records, the ambiguity-support table, and the hierarchyaudit table document evidence aggregation, conflict resolution, and hierarchy-derived changes. These files allow each sequence-endpoint state to be traced to its supporting sources and processing decisions. Metadata fields, controlled vocabularies, and data types are detailed in Supplementary Section S3.To support reproducibility, computational reuse, and long-term maintenance, MAOMAO was organized into complementary functional layers (Figure 1B). This modular architecture separates harmonized biological data, computational representations, benchmark resources, and supporting documentation while preserving interoperability across the resource.The Core Layer contains harmonized peptide sequences, toxicity annotations, ontology mappings, evidence classifications, provenance information, and metadata. It additionally provides numerical toxicity properties and sequence profiles. Descriptor-based representations were generated using Roxy (11), whereas embedding-based representations were obtained with Sylphy (12) using publicly available protein language models. Benchmark resources were generated using partitioning strategies implemented through BioSieve (10). The Documentation Layer contains ontology specifications, metadata schemas, resource descriptions, licensing information, and versioning records. Supported representations, benchmark resources, resource organization, and file structures are detailed in Supplementary Sections S4-S5.FAIR principles guided the design and construction of MAOMAO to support transparency, reproducibility, interoperability, and long-term sustainability. FAIR-oriented practices were incorporated across data collection, terminology harmonization, ontology development, evidence management, metadata integration, and resource organization.Interoperability and reusability were supported through standardized toxicity terminology, ontology-guided endpoint mapping, harmonized metadata schemas, explicit evidence categorization, provenance tracking, and version-aware organization. These components enable heterogeneous toxicity annotations to be integrated while preserving the original information associated with each record.Findability, accessibility, and computational reuse were supported by distributing resource components in machine-readable formats and using standardized identifiers linking sequences, annotations, metadata, ontology terms, and evidence categories. The sequence-derived SHA-256 identifiers provide a stable key for linking corresponding records across the Core, Descriptor, Embedding, Benchmark, and sequence-profile resources. Harmonization procedures, ontology definitions, evidence-management rules, metadata specifications, and generation workflows were also documented to support validation, updates, and downstream use. Resource availability, file organization, versioning, and supporting documentation are detailed in Supplementary Section S5.An overview of MAOMAO is presented in Figure 2A. The resource integrates toxicity-related information from 56 publicly available databases, literature-derived resources, supplementary datasets, and manually curated repositories. Of 1,372,190 non-deduplicated source-level records initially collected, 898,637 were retained after source-specific preprocessing, representing a reduction of approximately 34.5%. Removed records included duplicates, incomplete entries, formatting inconsistencies, and annotations that did not satisfy the inclusion criteria.Following terminology harmonization, ontology mapping, cross-source evidence aggregation, state resolution, and quality control, the final release comprised 71,857 unique peptide sequences across eight toxicity-related endpoints. These were organized into 574,856 sequence-endpoint combinations, together with standardized metadata and provenance records linking annotations, ontology assignments, evidence classifications, and source-specific information.Publication references, repository or server information, download dates, file formats, source types, and resource behavior were documented for all 56 sources. Annotation content and last-update dates were available for 55 sources (98.21%), whereas explicit licensing information was available for 15 sources (26.79%). Missing metadata were preserved without inference. These components provide a harmonized resource for organizing, disseminating, and computationally analyzing peptide toxicity information.The ontology-guided organization of toxicity annotations is presented in Figure 2B. The root category Toxic contains 57,080 available peptide-endpoint states, including 13,824 positives, and comprises four primary classes, namely Cytotoxic (25,454 available states; 7,122 positive), Neurotoxic (3,183; 1,481 positive), Embryotoxic (2 positive), and Ichthyotoxic (5 positive). The Cytotoxic branch is further divided into Hemolytic (35,960 available states; 4,714 positive), Cytolysis (343; 341 positive), and Anti mammalian cells (21,393 available states; 3,664 positive), preserving more specific biological contexts. These categories define the endpoint structure used throughout MAOMAO.Evidence-state distributions are summarized in Figure 2C and Supplementary Table S10. Across MAOMAO, 31,153 states were positive, 91,506 negative, 15,717 ambiguous, and 5,044 unlabeled. Because only positive annotations were propagated through the hierarchy, all other states remained endpoint-specific, and no-information states were excluded from the percentages shown in Figure 2C. Toxic contained 13,824 positives, whereas Hemolytic had the highest proportion of ambiguous states (19.05%) and was the only endpoint with unlabeled states, representing 14.03% of its available annotations.Across the seven non-root endpoints, 7,331 of the 9,421 peptides with at least one positive annotation were assigned to multiple toxicity categories. This corresponds to 77.82% of positive peptides across these endpoints and 10.2% of all MAOMAO sequences. Percentages were calculated relative to the positive sequences assigned to each row endpoint and should therefore be interpreted directionally. The largest overlap occurred between Cytotoxic and Hemolytic, with 4,128 shared sequences, representing 57.96% of cytotoxic-positive and 87.57% of hemolytic-positive sequences. Complete pairwise counts and directional percentages are provided in Supplementary Section S2.MAOMAO distributes harmonized annotations, numerical representations, benchmark resources, metadata, ontology definitions, and documentation across the functional layers shown in Figure 1B.The Core Layer contains 574,856 harmonized peptide-endpoint combinations corresponding to 71,857 unique sequences, together with ontology assignments, evidence classifications, provenance, and standardized metadata. It additionally provides 169 HC50, LC50, LD50, and MHC measurement records. Most were linked to the Core sequence universe, while six LD50 records remained unmatched because their sequences exceeded the 70-residue limit. One profile per Core sequence summarizes its activity annotations, supporting evidence, ontology effects, toxicity targets, selected descriptors, and available numerical toxicity properties. The Descriptor Layer provides 41 features capturing sequence composition and physicochemical properties.The Embedding Layer includes 10 protein-language-model embedding matrices and a one-hot representation, all covering the complete set of 71,857 MAOMAO sequences.The Benchmark Layer contains 300 endpoint-seed-strategy configurations generated through random and stratified five-fold partitioning of five eligible endpoints (Toxic, Cytotoxic, Hemolytic, Neurotoxic, and Anti mammalian cells) using 30 random seeds. These correspond to 1,500 data partitions and, across the 11 numerical representations, 3,300 representation-specific configurations and 16,500 fold instances. Associated parameters, reports, summaries, and execution records are also provided.The Documentation Layer includes ontology definitions, metadata schemas, resource descriptions, versioning records, and licensing information. Files are distributed in standard formats, including CSV, JSON, and YAML, with detailed component descriptions and inventories provided in Supplementary Sections S4-S5.To facilitate direct reuse of the distributed assets, MAOMAO provides five executable notebooks that operate on the released files rather than reconstructing the resource from the original sources. The introductory workflow covers resource access, file validation, navigation of the Core Layer, and linkage of annotations, numerical representations, and benchmark partitions through stable sequence identifiers. Complementary notebooks support descriptive characterization of endpoint states, class balance, co-occurrence, sequence lengths, ontology consistency, and representation coverage, as well as retrieval and querying of individual sequence profiles. Generated tables and figures are stored separately from the released resource files.Two additional notebooks illustrate downstream machine-learning reuse. The neurotoxicity classification example joins a released train-validation-test partition with an existing protein language model representation and evaluates logistic regression, a linear support vector machine, and random forest models using fixed settings. The quantitative regression example shows how MAOMAO's numerical toxicity measurements can be combined with a released sequence representation in a simple regression analysis. These workflows are intended to demonstrate resource interoperability and reproducible reuse rather than establish state-of-the-art predictors or replace the released benchmark design. Detailed descriptions of the demonstration notebooks, execution requirements, and generated outputs are provided in Supplementary Section S6MAOMAO was designed as a reusable resource for peptide toxicity research, providing a harmonized collection of toxicity annotations, ontology mappings, evidence classifications, metadata records, numerical representations, and benchmark resources. candidates.title: Fast Solution Methods for the Classical 0–1 Knapsack Problem
candidates.abstract: The classical 0--1 knapsack problem is among the simplest integer programs to state and among the most instructive problems for understanding why algorithm selection must follow instance structure. An input contains items with positive integer weights and profits, and the task is to choose a maximum-profit subset whose total weight does not exceed a capacity. The problem is weakly NP-hard, yet many large instances are solved quickly because exact algorithms exploit moderate numeric parameters, strong linear relaxations, dominance relations, or a small set of uncertain variables near the fractional break item. This review develops a theory-guided account of the principal fast solution methods for the classical problem. It proves the correctness and complexity of weight-indexed and profit-indexed dynamic programming, explains sparse Pareto-frontier implementations and reconstruction, derives the fractional-knapsack upper bound used by branch-and-bound methods, and establishes the correctness of meet-in-the-middle search. It then presents the core concept that underlies influential practical solvers and gives a detailed proof of the standard profit-scaling fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. Modern advances based on structured min-plus convolution are placed within this classical landscape rather than treated as isolated results. The central conclusion is that there is no universally fastest knapsack algorithm. Small item counts favor meet-in-the-middle search, moderate capacities or total profits favor dynamic programming, favorable density structure favors core-based exact methods, and very large numeric coefficients favor approximation. A final decision framework translates these theoretical distinctions into an implementable solver-selection policy while identifying open questions concerning adaptivity, certified switching among methods, memory efficiency, and realistic hard-instance generation.

candidates.title: Tipping point forecasting in nonstationary dynamics on function spaces
candidates.abstract: Tipping points are abrupt, drastic, and often irreversible changes in the evolution of nonstationary and chaotic dynamical systems. For instance, increased greenhouse gas concentrations are predicted to lead to drastic decreases in low cloud cover, referred to as a climatological tipping point. In this paper, we learn the evolution of such nonstationary dynamical systems using a recurrent neural operator (RNO), which learns mappings between function spaces. After training RNO on only the pre-tipping dynamics, we employ it to detect future tipping points using an uncertainty-based approach. In particular, we propose a conformal prediction framework to forecast tipping points by monitoring deviations from physics constraints (such as conserved quantities and partial differential equations), enabling forecasting of these abrupt changes along with a rigorous measure of uncertainty. We illustrate our proposed methodology on nonstationary ordinary and partial differential equations, such as the Lorenz-63 and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations. We also apply our methods to forecast a climate tipping point in stratocumulus cloud cover and airfoil wake and stall transitions using only limited knowledge of the governing equations. For the latter, we show that our proposed method zero-shot generalizes to forecasting multiple future tipping points under varying Reynolds numbers. In our experiments, we demonstrate that even partial or approximate physics constraints can be used to accurately forecast future tipping points.

candidates.title: Content-adaptive Multi-channel Hybrid Quantum-classical Block-wise Optimization for Robust Image Watermarking
candidates.abstract: The rapid growth of digital image distribution necessitates robust watermarking techniques to protect ownership and ensure data integrity.This paper proposes a content-adaptive hybrid quantum-classical watermarking framework that integrates local adaptive modeling and global optimization.The method employs Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) and Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to provide a stable embedding domain.Local texture features are extracted from image blocks and mapped using a trained Parameterized Quantum Circuit (PQC) to determine adaptive embedding strength.In parallel, Quantum-Inspired Annealing (QIA) is used to optimize the selection of DCT coefficient positions globally.A multi-channel embedding strategy is further incorporated to enhance robustness.Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves high imperceptibility (PSNR > 47 dB, SSIM ≈ 0.99) and strong robustness against the evaluated attacks, while remaining competitive with existing methods.The proposed framework provides a hybrid quantum-classical approach to image watermarking and represents a process innovation by integrating adaptive quantum learning with global coefficient-position optimization for robust multimedia copyright protection.

candidates.title: Reinforcement learning to disentangle multiqubit quantum states from partial observations
candidates.abstract: Using partial knowledge of a quantum state to control multiqubit entanglement is a largely unexplored paradigm in the emerging field of quantum interactive dynamics with the potential to address outstanding challenges in quantum state preparation and compression, quantum control, and quantum complexity. We present a deep reinforcement learning (RL) approach using an actor-critic algorithm for constructing short disentangling circuits for states with up to 16 qubits. With access to only two-qubit reduced density matrices, our agent decides which pairs of qubits to apply two-qubit gates on; requiring only local information makes it directly applicable on modern NISQ devices, as we demonstrated experimentally on a trapped-ion quantum computer. Utilizing a permutation-equivariant transformer architecture, the agent can autonomously identify qubit permutations within the state, and adjusts the disentangling protocol accordingly. Once trained, it provides circuits from different initial states without further optimization. We demonstrate the agent's ability to identify and exploit the entanglement structure of multi-qubit states. We analyze the disentangling circuits constructed by the agent for 4- and 5-qubit Haar-random states, and observe strong correlations between consecutive gates and among the qubits involved. Through extensive benchmarking, we show the efficacy of the RL approach to find disentangling protocols with minimal gate resources. We explore the resilience of our trained agents to noise, highlighting their potential for real-world quantum computing applications. Analyzing optimal disentangling protocols, we report a general circuit to prepare an arbitrary 4-qubit state using at most 5 two-qubit (10 CNOT) gates.

candidates.title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
candidates.abstract: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

candidates.title: Rational Design of a Photoactivated Fluorescent Probe for Thiol-ene Mediated Protein Labelling
candidates.abstract: Fluorescent labelling of biomolecules enables the visualization and tracking of molecular processes in cells, providing insights into cellular function and disease mechanisms. Despite recent advances in bioorthogonal labelling, efficient and site-selective strategies for targeting alkene functionalities remain limited. Here, we report AbzSH, a compact aminobenzamide-based fluorescent thiol probe for selective alkene labelling through thiol-ene ligation. Photoinduced ligation proceeds under mild, radical-mediated conditions in aqueous media and exhibits broad substrate compatibility, including carbohydrate, amino acid, and steroid scaffolds. The method is readily extended to protein labelling, enabling selective modification of both chemically functionalized proteins and engineered proteins containing genetically encoded alkene motifs. Efficient and chemoselective labelling was further demonstrated in complex cell lysates, highlighting the robustness of the approach in biologically relevant environments. Collectively, these results establish AbzSH as a versatile fluorescent probe for alkene-directed biomolecular labelling and provide a broadly applicable platform for chemical biology, molecular imaging, proteomics, and drug discovery.

candidates.title: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes. We propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks.
